name: Deinonychus
summary: Deinonychus are extremely aggressive , social and noisy small carnivores that live in groups called a dynasty when females are present - or troops when a group consists of all males. Dynasties are lead by a female - the Mother to all other females in the group - and experience a high level of behavioral dimorphism between the sexes. Males are low ranking, submissive, and expected to keep in line with hyper aggressive females, who fight and squabble amongst each other to gain favor with the Mother.
credits: Profile inspired by hyenas, meerkats, red-necked phalaropes & common dwarf mongoose.
quickView: Deinonychus are Small Diurnal Terrestrial Carnivores.
Deinonychus can group up to Unlimited sub/adults, unlimited offspring. Deinonychus do not adopt.

Groups with females are known as a dynasty, with all male groups referred to as a troop. A dynasty can have a maximum of 10 Unrelated males present, and a troop has a maximum of 10 males in it at a time.
Deinonychus can have up to 8 in an engagement or a hunting party.
Deinonychus may hunt up to Medium tier. With 4 members in a hunting party, they may hunt up to Large, and up to Apex tier with 8 members. They may scavenge, with limitations based on group size.
Deinonychus have a strict hierarchy where a single female, known as the mother, leads the group, known as a dynasty. Males form cooperative groups known as a troop if not part of a dynasty.
Some Deinonychus remain solitary indefinitely, preferring to trail behind large herds or apex carnivores for scavenging opportunities.

Female Deinonychus are the more aggressive of the two genders, living in a world of dominance, bullying, and aggressive behavior among one another. These behaviors are rewarded by other females, and sparring between individuals is common.
Males are more gentle, showing submission to females where possible, and enjoy gift giving and grooming behaviors. Groups comprised entirely of males, known as a troop, are gentle and cooperative.
Dynasties revolve around maternal lineage. Only the mother's daughters or sisters may nest. Granddaughters and nieces are not permitted to nest, and those caught doing so are exiled.
Related members in a Dynasty must individually log their relations in the  🩸・bloodline-logs to group together.

blocks.text: Small Diurnal Terrestrial Carnivore Though diurnal, they may perform all other activities during the night, except hunting, body contesting, and moving POIs. Deinonychus form temporary pairbonds. Deinonychus are nomadic. Deinonychus have an aggressive nature. Deinonychus may scavenge from claimed corpses and do not have to contest for a body when solitary, or in pairs. Groups of 3+ may only scavenge from Apex predator kills. Critters and abandoned corpses may be freely eaten. Deinonychus tolerate melanistics. Albinos are tolerated, but rank the lowest in the dynasty.

Skins that are considered mutations for Deinonychus include:: Any skin with "DRM" in the title Albino, Melanistic Players must roll in 🎲・genetics-rolls to use these skins in game. This is one roll per species, per character. Only when the character dies can you roll again if using the same character name.

Unlimited Sub/Adults, comprising of 1 dominant female known as the mother, 1 preferred male, related females, and males of any relation. A maximum of 10 Unrelated males can be present in a dynasty at any one time. Unlimited Offspring Deinonychus do not adopt. This group is known as a dynasty. Or: Up to 10 Sub/Adult males No offspring or adoptees This group is known as a troop. Additionally, Deinonychus may form dispersal groups may consisting of unlimited individuals of adolescent and below. These dispersal groups are sex specific and never mixed sex. Females must be related. Related members in a Dynasty must individually log their relations in the 🩸・bloodline-logs to group together. Players are responsible for logging their own characters.

Up to 8 Deinonychus may enter an engagement or hunt. If the group is attacked, individuals rush to protect the mother above all others. When nesting and with offspring under adolescent, the entire group may engage to defend the young. Engaged individuals must remain in line of sight of the nesting site. When defending a claimed body down, the entire group may engage. Deinonychus only hunt and contest for bodies during the day. Deinonychus may hunt up to Medium tier. With at least 4 in a hunting party, they may hunt up to Large tier. With a full hunting party of 8, they may hunt up to Apex tier. The mother and preferred male opt to sit out of hunts when there are enough hunting party members to take their place. Deinonychus do not tolerate scavengers. Deinonychus fear Quetzalcoatlus and Hatzegopteryx. They flee and scatter at the sight of these species, but may defend their kill or nesting site. They may attempt to defend the Mother - but once the Mother is safe, all Deinonychus prioritize fleeing over fighting. Deinonychus will attempt to cull unrelated and unattended offspring under adolescent. They receive no timers, and do not have hunger or time of day requirements to do this. Adolescent Deinonychus can assist with their parents’ hunts, up to the limit of 8. Solo Adolescent Deinonychus and dispersal groups have the same engagement limits as those in dynasty/troop. Preferred Prey Deinonychus may hunt up to Medium tier. With at least 4 in a hunting party, they may hunt up to Large tier. Deinonychus do not hunt Apex sauropods such as Apatosaurus. Solitary or paired Deinonychus may attempt to scavenge from any predator's kill. 3+ Deinonychus may only attempt to scavenge from Apex predator kills. Deinonychus are capable of expanding their diets to consume a range of foods when fresh meat is scarce. Particularly desperate individuals may resort to eating insects when no other food is available. Deinonychus target Tenontosaurus over any other prey if there are multiple prey options in the POI. Deinonychus may cull unattended Kelenken offspring under Sub-Adult without gaining a species timer, and can wipe out a full nest if able. They must flee if an Adult returns to defend the young. Deinonychus are unable to eat the bodies of Metriacanthosaurus without suffering averse side effects. See 📜・server-guideOPTIONAL - Illnesses & Injuries for more information.

🌧️ Rainy Season: 3 🥚 per 1 hour. ☀️ Dry Season: 5 🥚 per 1 hour. Deinonychus nest along cliff edges or deep inside caves. Their nests are constructed out of mud, reeds and roots, and decorated with thick ferns. Deinonychus males may form same-sex pairs, but do not adopt, and may still accept courtship from females. Deinonychus females become Elders after 20 clutches. Elders only have a maximum of 2 eggs per clutch, regardless of season. Nesting multipliers cannot be used on elder females. Albinos are infertile. Leucistics are fertile, but albino-appearing leucistics are rarely chosen as mates.

Deinonychus have no color dimorphism, and both sexes can be colorful or dull. ♀️ Females have head feathers. Suitable subspecies include: Apareonus, Jayens ♂️ Males have no head feathers. Suitable subspecies include: Antirrhopus Physical dimorphism for Deinonychus is not mandatory. However, males with headfeathers are never picked as mates by females or allowed in troops. Females without headfeathers are never respected by other females or able to start a dynasty. Females may display a temporary lack of headfeathers if they have been plucked in game. Non-dimorphic individuals still act as their biological sex. Others may be initially confused when first encountering them, but eventually learn - through scent, behavior and the reactions of others - the non-dimorphic's birth sex. Non-dimorphic females rank the same as plucked/Albino females.

Baby Deinonychus, known as fledglings, hatch out of their eggs either deep inside protected caves or up high on cliff edges. Fledglings require grooming shortly after hatching by an adult to help clean their feathers. Hatchling fledglings are quite noisy to ensure they are attended to, but settle down quickly after being cared for. They remain in the nest after this, recovering from the ordeal of hatching. By mid hatchling stage, fledglings begin to find their feet and start investigating other fledglings within the nesting territory. They nip at each other (and adults), play fight, and pick up whatever objects they can find. Fledglings do not leave the cave or away from the cliffside unless accompanied by an adult, and have food brought to them. Thus, when adults return to them, all fledglings mob them, squawking and begging for food. However, some persistent fledglings can be quite mischievous, and still attempt to leave the safety of the nesting site when they can sneak past. They are swiftly corrected and reprimanded by adults if this is spotted. The safest time of a Deinonychus' life is when they are a fledgling and born to the mother. These fledglings do not have to wait for the feeding hierarchy, and are permitted to eat as soon as the mother has taken her fill. The rest of the dynasty continuously bring them toys to keep them entertained. Fledglings run around with these objects, biting and throwing them around, and fighting to take them off other fledglings. Fledglings learn through mimicry. They watch adult females posture, growl and assert their dominance. Both female and male fledglings imitate these displays on siblings and objects they discover. Fledglings quickly learn what behaviors result in the best rewards for them. By adolescence, females fully understand that dominance is highly prized by the mother, and males become driven to show their submission, crouching and offering gifts to curry favor with the rest of the group. Male fledglings get lavished with affection from the adult males in the group. This attention and grooming helps prepare them for a more gentle life within the dynasty. Females, meanwhile, are doted on by their adult female relatives, particularly when they correctly show dominant behavior. Fledglings born to the mother have the highest rank out of all offspring. They are permitted to bully and harass other fledglings, which many of them take great delight in doing. Fledglings that attempt to bully and harass fledglings of the mother are always swiftly corrected by any adult that witnesses it. Fledglings who grow up without much adult care - such as those born to females that are not the mother, or orphaned at a young age - tend to be more skittish, opportunistic, and self-serving in adulthood. Forced to be more independent, they are more likely to develop rogue behaviors like hoarding food, and avoiding direct confrontation. Fledglings are permitted to leave the nesting site once they hit Adolescent stage, and are expected to fall in line with the rest of the dynasty to pull their weight. This includes participating in hunts, and following the strict feeding hierarchy after a kill. Any fledglings born to the mother's daughters or sisters must be introduced to her once they reach adolescence. Their mother must bring them forward, allowing the mother to inspect them - often with visible scrutiny - before begrudgingly accepting them into the dynasty. If fledglings are not properly introduced, they risk immediate exile or even death upon discovery. Any fledgling may be rejected by the mother - such as if she feels spited by said female introducing their offspring to her, or if the mother simply does not approve of the female's offspring. If these fledglings are born outside the dynasty, they are never accepted back into the original dynasty. Once fledglings reach Sub-Adult, they remain in the dynasty if the mother decides there is enough space. However, if the group reaches the mother's decided limit, or if the individual prefers to leave, the mother will drive them out, starting with: any related males, granddaughters, and nieces, in order to prioritize her daughters and potential breeding males. Sons of the mother may sometimes return to the dynasty if a space opens up, but they are always the first to be exiled again when room is needed. Grandsons and nephews, once exiled or dispersed, are not permitted to rejoin a dynasty. They may still share brief affectionate moments with their own mothers if encountered during migrations. Many related young males form troops, and travel together in search of new dynasties. Females strongly prefer to stay within the dynasty. The mother gives her daughters the highest priority to remain when she feels space is limited. If a daughter or sister leaves, she may return later if there is space, but must prove herself to regain the mother's favor. However, any daughters or sisters who have offspring outside the dynasty will find their young permanently rejected by the mother. Their children will not be allowed to join the dynasty under any circumstance and might get killed if introduced when they are still under adolescent. Granddaughters and nieces are not permitted to rejoin the dynasty that they dispersed from or were exiled out of. However, if their own mother (or sister) forms a dynasty, they may be permitted to join that dynasty.

Orphaned or driven out Deinonychus fledglings often struggle to survive. They steer clear of all other Deinonychus when possible, except their own same sex siblings, with which they will form a same sex dispersal group. If they are driven out of the dynasty at hatchling or juvenile stage, siblings will still break away into same sex dispersal groups. Orphaned fledglings without a dynasty - particularly those solo - can often be found trailing behind herds, hoping to scavenge whatever scraps they can. Same-sex dispersal groups travel widely and avoid confrontation, especially at younger ages. Keenly aware of the risk of cannibalization, they stick closely together, with disputes few and far between as individuals focus on their survival. Orphaned fledglings that survive to adulthood alone grow up wary, quiet, and fiercely independent. They struggle to connect with others and understand a lot of social cues - prompting harsh treatment if an orphaned male does not show proper submission to an adult female, or a lack of respect if a female is incapable of expressing correct dominance levels. Females end up forming their own dynasties later in life, with the most confident and dominant of a dispersal group emerging as the new mother. These dynasties often lack the social polish and maternal tolerance of those raised within a dynasty. These groups become especially aggressive nesters, prone to infanticide of each other's young. Males that never encounter females until adulthood often require a lot of correcting when they do encounter females. Without the usual education of being raised by females, they struggle to show submission at appropriate times - a lesson that is quickly and brutally learnt. If an offspring's mother dies Offspring to another female that is not the mother face a harsh reality if their mother dies. If these orphans are under adolescent, the mother will immediately turn on them. Orphans that cannot escape quick enough will be killed by the mother, with the rest of the dynasty joining in. However, orphans that are at least adolescent are permitted to remain in the dynasty. Deinonychus are quick and noisy dinosaurs. They spend a lot of their time posturing, hissing and squawking at one another and other dinosaurs they encounter. They rarely move silently, unless stalking prey or hiding. Deinonychus are nomadic, and spend their time travelling between their preferred POIs, with temporary overnight rest stops in caves or high up cliff sites. They spend time resting and napping in these temporary rest locations, with the mother in the safest position (usually the highest point, at the back, or in the middle of other dynasty members). She is flanked by her preferred male and favored daughters, and other females arrange themselves in closeness to her in order of seniority. Males are pushed to the outskirts, such as at the entrance of the cave and exposed positions. If a desirable cave or ledge is already occupied, Deinonychus approach in a loud and unified display. They spread their feathers, screech, lash their tails and hiss to try and intimidate the intruders into leaving. If this intimidating display fails, the group will escalate to actual aggression as they challenge for the spot. Both males and females are highly inquisitive, and interact with new objects, dinosaurs and experiences boldly. Some individuals can be more skittish than others - but curiosity lures even the shyest of Deinonychus into inspecting something new. Deinonychus spend a lot of time observing. Bound by their curious nature, they enjoy watching interactions between other species - including hunts, albeit from a safe distance! Vigilance over the group is a shared duty. While resting, males and lower ranking females take turns watching for danger. They perch up on high rocks or ledges, letting out distinctive alarm calls to warn the group if danger is spotted. Deinonychus do not like deep water. Their agility is hindered by swimming, and most individuals leap over streams or sprint along fallen logs or rocks to avoid getting wet. A misjudged jump results in loud, offended cries and frantic feather flapping as they paddle to safety. Dynasty members may scold individuals who get wet, adding insult to injury. On Riparia, Deinonychus inhabit many island POIs. They are more than capable of travelling across these islands without touching water in most cases. The most experienced individuals learn the best routes to take without having to swim. Deinonychus are diurnal hunters, but have a cathemeral bodyclock, requiring just short naps to recover. These naps are usually taken at night, when the entire group locates a resting area to settle in overnight. These areas are always a cave or cliff edge. Night time serves as a rest period for Deinonychus, but it does not consist of constant sleeping. This time is spent socializing, courting, scavenging and defending their temporary rest spot. Deinonychus do not migrate across POIs at night, and do not hunt at night.

Deinonychus tend to spend much of their downtime actively exploring their surroundings. While resting in one area, they observe nearby species and often interact with them - usually by being obnoxiously loud toward anything that ventures too close to their chosen spot. During downtime, most males engage in playful behavior and interact with one another. Females typically use this time to spar with other females or bond alongside males. Some may even feel comfortable enough to join in brief games of chase or to harass other females that choose to do so. Less playful individuals remain vigilant for potential threats, alerting the others to anything that draws near. Some choose to patrol the area alone, rejoining the group only when they require rest. Grandchildren, lower ranking females and males serve a particular use here. These individuals spend a lot of time scouting and patrolling the nearby area, and are quick to alert the rest of the dynasty to any potential threats. Those that prove themselves useful in these instances often find they win favor with the rest of the group. The mother typically assumes a watchful role over her Dynasty, interacting mainly with her chosen male or favored daughters during this time. These peaceful moments also offer the best opportunity for others to approach and grow closer to her.

The Mother Deinonychus groups that have females present have a strict social hierarchy that centers around a dominant head female, known as the mother. She is the most assertive and aggressive member of the group, and the one individual all other females are related to in some way. She is the main breeding female. The mother's authority is absolute, and her position is never challenged directly, and she does not pass leadership on to others. A dynasty is formed by one single female, sometimes alongside her sisters, and all other females within the group are either her descendants or close relatives. Her Offspring (Under Adolescent) The mother's recent offspring below adolescent rank directly below her. They receive the most affection and protection, and even poor behavior is often overlooked. The Preferred Male This is the mother's current chosen mate, who holds a unique position above all other adults, except her and the young in the group. He is allowed to sleep near her and eat before the other dynasty members. However, his status depends entirely on the mother's favor, and can be revoked at any time. Favored Daughters Daughters of the mother who have proven themselves through bullying, sparring, successful hunts or victories over rival dynasties are often favored by the mother, and become favored daughters. These daughters enjoy greater status, and often receive better treatment and access to food or nesting spaces. Favored Sons Sons of the mother that have proven especially loyal may be given a temporary favored son status when the group has a body. A maximum of one son may be chosen as 'favored' and allowed to eat from a corpse at the same time as the favored daughters. This position may switch each time the group has a body if the Mother has many sons she prefers. Favored Granddaughters Favored granddaughters are those chosen by the Mother, from offspring of the favored daughters. They rank just below their mothers as favored granddaughters. Other Female Relatives Remaining daughters and sisters of the mother fall next in the hierarchy. While still respected, they do not enjoy the same privileges as favored daughters. Other Offspring (Under Adolescent) Other juveniles and hatchlings within the group - those not directly born to the mother - come next. They are still given care and protection, but receive less tolerance for misbehavior. These are not permitted to be in the queue for food at a carcass. Their own mothers must wait their turn to be fed and then take a chunk for their offspring. Other Granddaughters & Nieces Other granddaughters and nieces rank next, and must wait patiently as their own mothers feed from the carcass before they may take their turn. All Other Males Males not selected as the mother's preferred male are lower ranking. Among them, unrelated males rank slightly higher than related males, as the dynasty prioritizes genetic diversity and will exile related males first when space is limited. Albinos, Non-Dimorphic Females & Plucked Females Regardless of sex or relation, albinos consistently rank at the very bottom of the hierarchy. They are shown less tolerance, and bullied by all other females within the group. This is the same for females who have been plucked and are still growing back their headfeathers. Hierarchy within a dynasty primarily determines the feeding order and how much favor an individual receives from the Mother. It is not a strict dominance hierarchy, and daughters are not expected to constantly submit to favored daughters - but may opt to do so to try and form alliances. Individual females of any rank or placing may spar, squabble and bully one another in order to compete for the Mother's attention. Granddaughters may spar with daughters, daughters may challenge favored daughters, etc. Females may harass and even bully the preferred male - so long as they are willing to face the consequences from the Mother if caught doing so! A female's rank reflects the Mother's preference, rather than social dominance over others.

All male groups are vastly different to groups containing females. Relationships between males are never as tense or based on dominance as they are among females. Troops do not have a strict rank system. While no male asserts dominance, others defer to the oldest or most confident individual, especially during migrations and when decisions must be made. This deference is subtle and not enforced. Males live in troops cooperatively. They groom each other frequently, share warmth during rest, and rarely fight. Disagreements are resolved through gentle shoving, vocal grumbles, or simply walking away. Meals are usually shared, with the finder or the one who landed the killing blow eating first. Hoarding or aggressing each other off of kills is extremely rare, usually reserved only for times when food is scarce. Troops are more cautious than dynasties. Without a female's natural aggression to back them, they avoid direct confrontations and often yield to larger predators or rival groups. However, they are clever and opportunistic, and adept at surviving by stealth and speed. Troops can consist of either related or unrelated males. Males often welcome other males into their group, but do not adopt or permit others below Sub-Adult to group with them.

Socialization within Deinonychus groups are complex and heavily influenced by sex and status. Males form deep, lifelong friendships with other males. It's not uncommon to see pairs resting with their necks draped over one another, or grooming for extended periods. Same sex bonds between males frequently occur due to this closeness. These males spend nearly all their time together, and express deep sorrow at the loss of a partner. Despite this, partnered males may still accept courtship advances from a female within a dynasty, but quickly go back to their male partner afterwards. Male relationships are generally peaceful, with disagreements resolved very differently to female disputes. Rather than fighting, males tend to express their frustration through avoidance, sulking, and withdrawing affection. A male who feels neglected may refuse to groom his companion, deliberately sit apart from them, or ignore attempts at social interaction until the relationship - or issue - is repaired. Female social dynamics are far more volatile. While some friendships between females form, competition is a constant undercurrent. Jealousy between females is common. Females often dislike sharing a male, particularly with sisters or daughters, and fights over courtship, grooming attention, and even sleeping spots are frequent. Likewise, jealousy is equally common in males, particularly when a close companion begins to spend more time with another individual. Unlike females, this never escalates into violence. However, males do not interfere with female choices - though they may reject courtship - and do not compete for status among themselves. Males may frequently feel jealousy among each other if a female picks another male over them. Some males may resort to sneaky tactics - such as covertly stealing a gift out from under another male - to present to a female. Lower-ranking females, especially those overlooked by the mother, often band together. These small alliances serve as both emotional support and a strategic effort. They groom each other, share scraps, and collectively work together to isolate a rival in an attempt to climb the social ladder. Alliances among females are fragile, however. A female who begins to gain the mother's favor may be turned on by her former companions in a scramble for status. Female friendships are often tested by courtship conflicts. If a male gifts a female or overly grooms her - and the other female had grown possessive over that male - that female may respond jealously with tail-fanning, biting, or shunning both the male and female temporarily. Social grooming is frequent and reinforces bonds between individuals. While most feather preening is self-directed, close individuals (especially males to other males, or males to females they are trying to win favor with) groom one another regularly. Grooming is also used to calm group tensions after disputes.

Within a dynasty, females often form powerful bonds with a particular sister - or, more commonly, their own daughters. As a result, nesting is crucial for most daughters, ensuring they raise potential allies that can help improve their status and provide support against other females in the group. These females often band together and form tightknit cliques. They groom one another and work together to isolate, harass and undermine other females in an effort to increase their own influence with the Mother.

Within a dynasty, males earn favor from females through visible acts of submission, and presenting gifts. Not all males participate in gift giving, but those that do more quickly earn favor. Submission is displayed by crouching when approached by a female. Females frequently test this behavior by standing over a male, waiting silently. If the male crouches promptly, she rewards him with an affectionate headshake. If he hesitates - or worse, fails to crouch at all - she will hiss at him, fanning her tail in irritation. Males only show this behavior towards females. Males do not perform submissive acts to other males, but may still gift other males as an act of affection. Males are active gift-givers, and bring interesting items they find to females, offspring, and even other males, as a form of social bonding. These gifts can include shiny stones, colorful flowers, nesting material or scraps of food - each chosen for its visual appeal or scent. Preferences vary widely between individuals, pushing males to be observant and creative with gifts they choose. When given a gift, males respond with warmth, offering grooming and gentle chirps of appreciation. Females are more selective. If pleased, a female takes the item with her and lavishes the male with affection in return. But if the gift disappoints her, she will rudely discard it, often by flinging it aside, and express her annoyance by flaring out her feathers, and tail-fanning in the male's direction. For males, successful submission and gift giving are often the key to acceptance, and winning favor with females.

Related males have little influence over the dynasty's decisions, but may attempt to sabotage unrelated males they dislike. This is most commonly done by stealing, hiding or damaging gifts intended for females, particularly if the suitor is courting the male's mother or sisters. By reducing the quality of a rival's offerings, the related male can make him appear less desirable. Related males may also assist unrelated males that they do like and wish to keep within the dynasty. Having grown up alongside the females, related males often know which gifts are most likely to be appreciated. They may help favored suitors locate suitable offerings to provide assistance during courtship, or accompany them while gathering gifts.

sections.title: The dynasty when the mother is unavailable

blocks.text: A dynasty can continue its movements when the mother is temporarily unavailable. A favored daughter leads the dynasty in her stead, but a spot is always reserved for the mother's return. Any offspring born when the mother is not present risk being exiled on her return. The mothers of these offspring must be quick to introduce them to her as soon as possible to prevent this happening.

Albino Deinonychus rank the lowest in every dynasty. Male albinos are never accepted as mates by females, and only exist within a dynasty by being born into one. Female albinos may start out as aggressive as their sisters, but over time they are repeatedly brought down by their sisters and the Mother. All albinos eventually become extremely submissive, and attempt to be as unassuming as possible as a survival measure. They show no aggression, and forfeit immediately if challenged by other females. Mothers never tolerate any aggression from albino females, and always correct this. Males aggressed by an albino female are not expected to submit but may still choose to crouch and accept her frustrations. Others quickly move away from an aggressing albino female, further within the dynasty, knowing the behavior will be reprimanded by those above her. This also applies to non-dimorphic females and plucked females. Female albinos, however, are still accepted as mates by males, but are unable to produce eggs. They rank the lowest within a dynasty, and come absolute last in the feeding hierarchy. Some mothers may opt to stop any interactions between albino females and unrelated males. Troops and solitary males choose not to group with Albino females unless part of a larger dynasty.

If these individuals have a visual similarity to albinos, they are treated in the same way. They are unable to establish their own dynasties like albinos, as males in the wild consistently dismiss solitary albino or albino-appearing leucistic individuals in favor of seeking potential mates and companions elsewhere.

Solo Deinonychus are more quiet and cautious than those within troops or dynasties. They avoid unnecessary conflict, learning to rely on stealth, patience, and careful observation to survive. They tend to shadow larger herbivores and apex predators from a distance, hoping to scavenge from kills, or glean safety by association. However, they remain ready to flee at the first sign of hostility. Solitary individuals spend a lot of time watching, learning from the behavior of other species and honing their hunting skills through trial and error. Though they may still attempt hunting, scavenging is the most common way a solitary Deinonychus manages to feed itself. Orphans or exiles from dynasties display high levels of anxiety, often vocalizing when alone. Some solitary males may attempt to join existing dynasties as potential mates, or even band together with other males in a troop. However, some prefer to remain alone. Solitary females can only start a dynasty on their own with another male. They are not accepted into other dynasties.

When a strange Deinonychus is spotted by the rest of the dynasty, a scout calls out the alarm to draw the group close. The mother - or favored daughter, if the mother is not present - steps forward to inspect the new male, or male troop. Other dynasty members are aggressively called from getting too close, but remain nearby, slowly forming a circle around the newcomers. The mother inspects closely, looking over the newcomer and sniffing to take their scent. Should they be crouched and showing appropriate submission - and the dynasty has room - the mother will shake her head over him, before barking to invite the rest of the group in. The dynasty then descends on the newcomer like a swarm, moving close and sniffing to inspect. This introduction can be very alarming - especially for young, inexperienced males - but is part of how a dynasty welcomes in a new male. If there is no room, or the male does not show appropriate submission or the mother takes a disliking to him, he is swiftly aggress called :threaten_call: by the mother, which prompts a chorus of aggressive calling from the rest of the dynasty, who move to chase him out of the POI. If a favored daughter accepts a new male member in the mother's absence, the mother will repeat the introduction with the new males over again, and may opt to exile them if they do not meet her approval. If there are more males than the dynasty has room for, the mother may be selective on which males she accepts. This selection can unfortunately part bonded males - who may opt to leave with their male partner rather than be parted from him.

sections.title: Troops or solo males encountering other males

blocks.text: Male encounters are cautious, but much less aggressive than introductions involving a female. Full troops of 10 members do not engage, preferring to observe briefly before moving on. If open to newcomers, the oldest or most confident male approaches first, chirping and shaking to gently inspect him. The newcomer does not crouch as he would for females, but offers friendly headshakes and soft calls in return. The rest of the troop then approach, and if accepted by all parties, the troop include the new male in their group. They settle somewhere nearby and begin a ritual of deep, group-lead grooming, with individuals focusing on the newcomer. If a male with head feathers attempts to join a troop, the troop reacts with confusion and will immediately flee, unwilling to risk being misidentified as a dynasty or drawing aggression from females during a possible encounter. Mothers lead their dynasty with an iron fist and expect submission at all times. Individuals that show disobedience or lack of respect towards the mother are sharply scolded, and repeat offences may cause them to be kicked out of the dynasty. If the offending female has fledglings, the mother may choose to slaughter them if she feels she has been slighted too many times. The mother chooses favorite daughters, and will prioritise them when sharing food. The decision for how a mother chooses a favorite daughter is down to the individual - but usually bullying and beating the other females in the group and proving themselves as adept hunters is the easiest way to secure the position. Favored daughters often develop preferences among their own offspring, investing more time and resources into certain daughters who they believe have the best potential. These young daughters are frequently groomed, defended, and encouraged to rise through the dynasty's hierarchy. However, only the Mother decides which granddaughters are granted the status of favored granddaughter. Favored granddaughters can only come from the offspring of favored daughters, and enjoy increased protection, access to food and higher influence within the group. This can sometimes create tension between the Mother and her favored daughters. A favored daughter may invest heavily in one offspring, only for the Mother to show preference towards a different granddaughter. In these situations, the daughter is forced to support the Mother's chosen favorite regardless, as opposing the decision risks damaging her own standing. A favored granddaughter's position - like a favored daughter's position - is never guaranteed. Should she repeatedly disappoint the Mother, her favored status may be revoked. In extreme cases, the Mother may also question the judgement of the favored daughter who produced and supported her, potentially resulting in both granddaughter and daughter losing their favored status within the dynasty. Because favored granddaughters gain their status entirely through their mother's position, they immediately lose their standing if their mother loses her place as a favored daughter. Deinonychus females, as a result, display bullying behavior to one another, vying for a position as a favorite female under the mother's eye, as well as over access to resources and particular males. Bullying involves shoving, getting in their personal space, air snapping, stealing meat, blocking their path as they move, rushing to take a preferred sleeping spot, flirting with their courting partner, and generally being annoying and disruptive. Some females may even go so far as to nip potential rivals or males that have provoked their irritation. This is a carefully measured action, as others that witness this may step in to defend the individual - or prompt the individual into challenging back. Bullying is always met with either submission or bullying back, but if one individual has had enough of repeated instances, it escalates to a quick fight known as a spar, detailed below. In extreme cases the bullying may escalate to the deliberate plucking of head feathers. This is considered severe social punishment and can leave a female partially or entirely bald, increasing the risk of her being mistaken for a male. While head feathers may eventually regrow, the process takes time - at least one full in game day cycle. Females lacking head feathers for extended periods are heavily bullied and will be deranked to as low as being treated similarly to albino individuals. During this time the female switches to the Antirrhopus sub-species to showcase their lack of head feathers. Some females may attempt to bully or harass the mother’s preferred male when the mother is not present, testing his position or venting jealousy. If the mother discovers this behavior, she responds with severe aggression, often resulting in serious injury to the offender. Repeated or bold offenses can result in immediate exile from the dynasty, but after a while this female may be allowed to return.

Sparring is frequent within a dynasty between females - but nobody ever challenges the mother. To begin a challenge, a female approaches the other female, circling and locking eyes with her. If the opponent accepts the challenge, she will meet her gaze with an intense stare, and both females start to circle, making sure to keep eyes on one another. If neither female is intimidated, they escalate it further, and rush forward with a series of tail fanning, shoving, air snapping and aggressive calls. Finally, the challenge escalates into a full fight, with both females rushing at the other and biting, clawing and slashing at one another. This fight continues until one female reaches half health, marking her as the loser. She crouches and cries out to announce her submission, and the mother - if she witnessed the fight - moves forward to show her approval to the victor. The loser may be ignored by the mother for a short while, showcasing her displeasure. A female that continues fighting after one reaches half health is quickly reprimanded by the rest of the dynasty - including the mother. Repeated offences can result in her exile. Females cannot challenge the same opponent again for 15 minutes, but may challenge others during this time to try and regain the mother's favor. Losers avoid the victor during this time. This timer still applies even if a female forfeits during a spar.

While most disputes are settled through individual sparring between females, entire female alliances may occasionally challenge one another. Alliance sparring can involve up to three females per side, with the winning side crowned by the last female to reach half health. These alliance spars can be fought as: 3 females x 3 females 3 females x 2 females 2 females x 2 females These spars begin the same way as individual sparring. If an individual female is challenged by an alliance of 2-3 females, she immediately submits or flees if she is unable to gather her own support. The Mother may break up alliance spars before they start to allow 1v1 spars if she wishes. Losing females may turn to immediately bullying other, lower-ranking females or males afterwards.
Plucked females may participate in individual sparring and alliance sparring, but do not gain favor for winning these battles. Others will not submit to them even when beaten.

Plucking amongst females is considered a serious offence. While usually only performed by the Mother, in some cases other females may pluck other females if they have been offended by these individuals too many times. Females that repeatedly challenge another female and consequently lose more than 3 times in a row against that female may be plucked by the victor. Females that are challenged and lose 3 times in a row do not get their head feathers plucked by the victor.

Used exclusively by females, tail-fanning directly into an offender is a clear display of disapproval or irritation. Deinonychus females direct this at individuals who are too close, behaving improperly, or are otherwise deserving (in the female's eyes) of scolding. The gesture serves as a warning to back off without escalating into physical violence.

sections.title: Encountering a Rival Dynasty or Females

blocks.text: All rival females are immediately chased out of the POI. Although Deinonychus females are not territorial, they do not tolerate other females to occupy the biome they are currently residing in - especially if they have fledglings. When a dynasty encounters another dynasty, both sides will call for the mother - or favored female in command - and both groups will arrive, sizing each other up with cold stares and posturing. If one dynasty has significantly less members than another (4 or more), that dynasty opts to forfeit by fleeing the POI - escorted out by the vicious calls of the victorious dynasty. If numbers are similar, a battle for the right to remain in the POI occurs. The mother - or favored female in command - sits out of these fights unless there are less than 8 others available to engage. Deinonychus do not start territory challenges versus another Dynasty until after the mother/favored daughter at the head of both sides has moved out of the way of the incoming engagement. Fights then begin, with up to 8 members on either side, and continue until a body drops or one side forfeits. Forfeits must be accompanied with fear calls and fleeing - those that linger too long risk facing the wrath of the dynasty.

Unrelated and unattended offspring under adolescent can be killed on sight, without any hunger or time of day requirements, and give no timers to the attackers. Both males and females will cannibalize unrelated offspring in this way.

Males are generally free to leave a dynasty at will, and often do so - especially if they have gone multiple seasons without being chosen for nesting. Dispersal for males is typically quiet. Males tend to slip away unnoticed, often during moments when the dynasty is distracted, such as during travel, feeding, or following a confrontation. Males rarely make formal goodbyes. Their departures are casual and non-disruptive, and the rest of the group usually does not chase them or stop them. Many males leave in pairs or small groups, especially if they have formed strong bonds with other males. These companions may go on to form a troop together. Occasionally, a particularly cunning male can lead a dual life, quietly moving between two dynasties, and nesting with multiple females. This type of behavior is rare, simply due to the demands placed on the male to support multiple females. Unrelated males can be welcomed back into a dynasty at any time, at the whim of the mother. Related males are only allowed back in if they are the direct sons of the mother. Males that witness a rival dynasty besting the one they are part of may choose to disperse later, and track down the winning dynasty.

Female dispersal is rare. Dynasties are matriarchal and protective of lineage, and females are expected to remain loyal unless exiled. A female may choose to leave only under extreme circumstances - usually due to repeated scolding by the mother, excessive bullying from peers, or consistently being passed over for status or breeding. Females slip away in a manner similar to males, and are sometimes accompanied by a sister or daughter. As they cannot join other dynasties, those who leave must form their own. Females who attempt to return to their original dynasty are rarely welcomed. Only daughters or sisters of the mother are welcomed back in, while granddaughters and nieces are rejected. However, granddaughters and nieces may be permitted to join their own mother's dynasty.

The death of the mother is the most destabilizing event a dynasty can experience. As the core of its structure, her absence throws the entire group into uncertainty and disorder. Without her presence, the dynasty loses its center. The feeding order collapses, sleeping arrangements are disrupted, and formerly submissive females begin testing boundaries. Vocalizations increase sharply as females posture and aggressive call at one another, with pacing and challenging increasing. Adult daughters, sisters and other close female relatives begin vying for control. These power struggles are not fatal - females fight until one is reduced to deathscars, forcing the other to submit. However, these conflicts are numerous, often with one single female fighting the entirety of the rest of the group to grapple for ultimate control. If no clear successor emerges, or the infighting becomes too intense, the dynasty may split entirely. Small factions form around strong female personalities, with daughters and sisters to each other grouping to form several smaller dynasties. Once a new successor emerges, the new mother must exile more distant relatives. Only the new mother's sisters and offspring are permitted to remain. Nieces, nephews, brothers and any other relations must be exiled from the dynasty. In rare cases, a new mother may allow her father back into the dynasty if she has bonded with him well since youth. He receives no special role and can be pushed out like other related males if the mother deems the group full, but may return at a later time. The father to the mother is not permitted to court any females, as he is related to all of them. Males prefer to leave quietly during the turmoil of a new dynasty formation. They band together in a protective group, waiting on the outskirts so as not to get involved in any disputes. If the Mother has offspring under adolescent These orphaned young experience extreme neglect, and are either killed or exiled by their adult sisters and female relatives. The surviving orphans have to become as independent as possible, and learn scavenging and hunting in order to stay fed but may not remain in the dynasty if below adolescent. Deinonychus are extremely noisy and rude neighbours to almost all other dinosaurs in their vicinity. When groups come across another dinosaur in their travels, they launch into a loud and aggressive display while keeping a safe distance. This involves posturing, loud calls, and mock-attacks into the air. Deinonychus are all bark and no bite in these situations - unless planning to hunt the other species. As soon as the other dinosaur starts to approach, they flee the scene and retreat to the safety of a cave or cliff edge if possible. Caves and cliff edges are temporarily claimed by Deinonychus and any dinosaur challenging their resting spot or attempting to enter will be met with deadly force of the entire group. These resting locations are protected defensively while in use, and Deinonychus will not chase dinosaurs further than LOS of the area; retreating back if the dinosaur leaves. If a spot they have chosen already has an occupant, they will attempt to root out the dinosaur so that they may use it for resting at night, or nesting. Deinonychus will attempt to follow Tyrannosaurus and Giganotosaurus where possible in the hopes of being able to scavenge from their kills. The larger the dynasty, the less likely they are to be tolerated - though this doesn't stop them from trying! They will heed warnings when given by these Apex carnivores, and keep their distance if threatened. Deinonychus scatter and flee at the sight of Hatzegopteryx or Quetzalcoatlus. They almost never engage with either of these unless cornered, with a body or at a claimed nesting site. Deinonychus do not tolerate Compsognathus, Rhamphorhynchus or any scavengers, and aggressively chase them away. If lucky enough to discover an unattended nest of Kelenken chicks under adolescent, Deinonychus can slaughter the entire brood without incurring species timers. However, if an adult comes to defend them, Deinonychus gives up this feat and flees. Deinonychus are especially adept hunters of Tenontosaurus, and always target this prey species first if multiple prey options are in the POI. Deinonychus may attempt to provide grooming opportunities to Anodontosaurus and sauropods, if tolerated. Latenivenatrix are not tolerated in the same POI. If a Deinonychus group is resting in a POI, they will try to chase out any Latenivenatrix. Solitary Deinonychus avoid conflict with Latenivenatrix.

Some Deinonychus learn through experience that Citipati are a species that can prove unexpectedly useful companions. Female Citipati are known to become intensely broody, and often target other smaller dinosaurs to treat as surrogate Citipati offspring. While this confusion can seem alarming at first, clever Deinonychus learn to play along - taking advantage of the Citipati's protective instincts to gain access to food, shelter and defence. When tolerated or even "adopted" by the unwitting female Citipati, Deinonychus often signal to others within its dynasty or troop, leading to entire groups descending on a single unsuspecting Citipati. These swarms act harmless at first, feigning juvenile behaviors. This tolerance is never out of affection. The true motive behind such behavior is often the herbivore herds that Citipati travel with. Deinonychus may linger near Citipati specifically to hunt their companions, using the association as camouflage or distraction. To maintain their position, Deinonychus may actively target Citipati roosters and offspring. Roosters often recognize the deception and will attempt to separate the female from her adopted "young", driving the Deinonychus off aggressively. As such, they are considered a direct threat and are typically harassed or hunted first. Likewise, Citipati chicks can divert the female's attention and transfer her maternal instincts away from the Deinonychus. If present, they are swiftly removed when the female Citipati's back is turned.

Latenivenatrix are not tolerated in the same POI. If a Deinonychus group is resting in a POI, they will they will try to chase out any Latenivenatrix. When Deinonychus spot Latenivenatrix in the POI, members of the dynasty or troop with call loudly to gather the rest of its group. Should Latenivenatrix flee immediately, Deinonychus will chase them from the POI with vicious calls. If Latenivenatrix do not flee, this begins a territory challenge if Deinonychus does not opt to flee themselves. The entire dynasty or troop may posture and call, up to 8 Deinonychus then launch the attack. Deinonychus do not hunt Latenivenatrix. Deinonychus must challenge the Latenivenatrix out, or flee the POI. Solitary Deinonychus avoid conflict with Latenivenatrix. Deinonychus form a hunting party of up to 8 Adolescent and above individuals - though Sub-Adult+ are preferred. If the hunting party has enough dynasty members to fill this number, the mother and preferred male will not participate during the hunt. Deinonychus can hunt up to Medium tier, but this is expanded to Large tier with at least 4 in a hunting party. With a full hunting party of 8, they may hunt Apex tier - but do not attempt to hunt Apex sauropod species. Prey is scoped out by multiple Deinonychus in a dynasty or troop, who keep tabs and whereabouts of potential prey options, assessing the likelihood of success. Once a target has been successfully acquired, Deinonychus call loudly to draw in the rest of the hunting party, who rush in to swarm the target. Hunts are usually quick and highly coordinated. Members jump and latch onto targets in great numbers, biting and slashing them with their claws. Once a hunt is successful, one member of the dynasty leaves to find the mother (should she not have been present for the hunt), to bring her to the kill before any of the others are permitted to eat. As soon as a kill is made, males quickly race to collect the trophy from the body if possible, hoping to utilize it as an especially impressive gift later on. This is tolerated by the females in the group, but a female with a temporary grudge against one of the males may deliberately opt to take it before that male can. The mother eats her fill first while the rest of the dynasty watches, waiting patiently for their turn. After she is satiated, the mother approaches members of the dynasty to allow them to eat, barking an affectionate call to signal that their turn has come. The feeding order follows with: Any of the mother's offspring under adolescent Her preferred male Favored daughters Favored granddaughters Daughters Other female relatives, including sisters, granddaughters, and nieces Males Albinos, Leucistics that appear Albino, and females without head feathers Sometimes, feeding in this way means the members ranking at the bottom of the hierarchy frequently go without a meal. These individuals are often forced to scavenge to avoid starving. If the Mother is not present, bold - or desperate - individuals may attempt to skip the feeding order, but are typically harshly reprimanded by the rest of the group if witnessed. Some individuals rush to collect the Mother to alert her of this behavior, whilst hoping to gain favor themselves. Any member that tries to eat before it is their turn is swiftly reprimanded by the rest of the group. The mother may choose to entirely deny food to a particular member, regardless of ranking, if they have displeased her. Females that have offspring under adolescent have to wait their turn before they can feed their young. Once it is their turn to eat, they usually take a chunk from the body to deliver to their waiting fledglings. In a troop, males do not have a strict feeding order, and all males are permitted to eat from the body at the same time.

Courtship within a dynasty is a slow, subtle process that begins with social bonding, rather than direct competition. Males invest significant time building relationships with females - and each other - through gift giving, grooming, and consistent displays of submission - especially towards the mother and favored daughters. Affection is expressed gently. Males offer grooming during rest periods, bring small gifts to fledglings, and watch over the group with quiet attentiveness. These behaviors serve not only to demonstrate worth, but to foster emotional connections. Females develop preferences naturally over time, gravitating toward males who make them feel respected and admired. Males seeking favor may increase their attentiveness, courting the mother with exceptional submission, grooming favored daughters, or trying to position themselves closer to the center of group activity to be more visible. Gifting a hunting trophy to a female is a very prestigious gift, and always secures appreciation when presented as an offering.

When a female is ready to nest, she approaches her chosen male with a unique display. She spreads her arms wide, turns in a tight circle, and calls to him affectionately. If the male accepts her advances - and is crouched, showing submission appropriately - he rises to mirror her gestures. If he rejects her, he lets out a quiet, submissive noise, and turns to slowly move away. Rejected females may take offense, but never force a bond. Instead, they withdraw their attention from the male - sometimes even shunning him for a short period - and transfers her affection onto another male. Females may both like the same male in some instances. On these occasions, they may spar for the right to court him.

Granddaughters and nieces are never permitted to nest. If caught courting - or worse, actually nesting in offspring - they may be exiled (temporarily or permanently), and their offspring slaughtered upon discovery. The mother nests only with her preferred male, with no other female allowed access to him. Attempts to court him are punished, and the mother will drive away both males and females who get too close to her preferred male. Sometimes, females may sneakily nest with the preferred male, when the mother's back is turned. If the female manages to raise the offspring to adolescence without the mother noticing, they are often accepted unknowingly. However, if caught, the female and the preferred male face the mother's wrath. She almost always attempts to cull the offspring, and may temporarily - or even permanently - exile one or both offenders. Any parents attempting to sneaky nest should leave their children out of the in-game group until they are adolescent. Females who displease the mother are blocked from nesting entirely. Attempts to court are interrupted and stopped, with both individuals reprimanded swiftly. In extreme cases, the mother may deliberately choose a female's male partner as her next preferred male. In contrast, females who remain in good standing are usually permitted to nest. The mother encourages maternal behavior within her dynasty with leading by example, believing that a nurturing environment increases the survival and success of her own bloodline.

Same sex courting does not have an overall, direct process between males. It is slow burning and builds over time, much like with females, but is often laster longing. Presenting another male with a hunting trophy helps secure a partnership between two males. This prestigious gift is very valuable, and holds a lot of weight, particularly among other males who might use them to garner favor from a female. Same-sex couples spend much of their time together, and particularly enjoy being caretakers to any fledglings within the dynasty. Same-sex males still keep the instinct to pass on their genetics, and may accept courting from females when approached - but quickly return to their male partner after.

Deinonychus always nest inside a cave or the edge of a cliff side. These locations are fiercely protected by all members of the dynasty from any unwelcome intrusion. Deinonychus surround their nests with thick ferns. The mother gets the most desirable nesting site within the cave, and will never share a nesting spot close to other females. If an area only has one spot, the other females must wait until she has finished using it, or find a new location nearby in order to nest in their offspring. Other females never challenge the mother for an area to place their nest. However, they may challenge one another in the form of a sparring match. Once the mother's fledglings are born, all members of the Deinonychus dynasty help out with rearing them. They bring them food and gifts, accompany them to water, and defend them from any threats. Mother fledglings essentially live a very comfortable and protected life. Other females that are nesting are not permitted to mix their fledglings with the mother's until they are at least juvenile. They receive no help from other dynasty members in rearing their babies, and are expected to pitch in with the mother's fledglings as well as their own. Any female seen prioritising her own brood rather than the Mother's will receive harsh punishment from the rest of the dynasty - such as shunning behavior or even aggression from the mother herself. Due to having to provide for both the mother's fledglings and her own, a female that nests at the same time as the mother may only be able to raise one or two fledglings as the others may starve. In extreme circumstances, a female may opt to reduce her brood through culling to ease the pressure. Males - especially males that have courted and nested in offspring this season - assist by bringing prey and scraps for fledglings, collecting small objects as makeshift "toys", and gently grooming and playing with young to build early trust. Males lavish affection on male offspring especially, helping to guide them with submissive behavior in order to win over the approval of females. Fledglings that tumble out of the nest may be gathered up by males, but sometimes get rejected by the mother. This rejection is not a death sentence, but forces fledglings to work harder to gain her favor. Once fledglings reach Adolescent, they are treated as adult members of the dynasty. They are expected to help raise other fledglings, hunt, and socialise with the other adults.

It can be difficult for daughters to determine whether the mother will allow them to nest, so many opt to show courting behavior - and general affection towards their chosen males - in front of the Mother in order to gauge her reactions. Mothers that witness this and do not move to stop or aggress the couple can generally be presumed as accepting of the daughter's willingness to nest. However, granddaughters, albino-appearing leucistics, females that desire the preferred male and females not permitted to nest may opt to do so in the form of a Sneaky Nest. This is by disappearing to nest quietly and maintaining appearances whilst keeping their clutch concealed. Closely bonded females may turn a blind eye if catching one another sneaky nesting. Whilst others race to inform the Mother - and therefore improve their standing while weakening their rivals' - these strongly bonded females may stay quiet instead. Mothers of sneaky nests are more cautious and wary of their surroundings - understanding that being caught by the Mother - or worse, a sibling who could rouse her - will mean the slaughter of her fledglings. Fathers do their best to provide for both the sneaky nest and the Mother as usual, but preferred males face additional risk if caught tending to another female's nest. As such, some preferred males may choose to distance themselves from the sneaky nest to protect against suspicion. Most females feel extreme stress levels when tending to a loud brood within a sneaky nest. Extremely loud offspring that do not follow commands may even be culled by her, in effort to preserve the rest of the clutch. Additionally, females who get caught by a vengeful sister may opt to cull her young before the Mother returns to discover them. Allied and closely bonded females may help each other conceal sneaky nests from the Mother. This is a particularly risky investment - as either female could betray the other, and both may face consequences if caught by the Mother. Granddaughters may work with their mother and nest at the same time to try and pass a maximum of 1 offspring as their mother's, by mixing them in her nest. Some may attempt to do so without their mother's permission, risking the chick being culled if discovered. Others may be indulged by their mother and allowed to mix the broods. Once offspring reach Adolescent, what happens next is determined by the mother of the clutch's position, and her preferences: Granddaughters that have nested alone must disperse her offspring. They cannot join the dynasty, but may join the granddaughter if she - or her mother - establish a dynasty of their own. Should the offspring have successfully passed off as their mother's, they may stay within the dynasty, considered as grandchildren. This must be noted in the bloodline log clearly. Albino-appearing leucistics must disperse her offspring, regardless of whether they are daughters or granddaughters themselves. Daughters that have nested with the preferred male may present their offspring as normal, with the father absent. Young that appear very similar to the father visually may be chased out of the dynasty by their mother to prevent the Mother discovering the secret. Daughters who were not given permission to nest may attempt to present their offspring as normal - often accompanying the presentation with a gift to help soften the Mother's mood. There is no guarantee the Mother will accept them, so some may prefer to disperse them. When females disperse their offspring to avoid getting caught, they do so by shunning them, escalating quickly into aggression - and even attacks - if the young do not get the message and linger. Nesting as an Albino-Appearing Individual: All individuals that are Albino-appearing do not suffer the same fertility issues as Albino individuals. However, if discovered by any other individuals in the Dynasty, the mother is quickly alerted, and the chicks are culled. This may result in a complete exile of the Albino-appearing individual and their mate, or aggressive bullying by all the females within the Dynasty. As Deinonychus age, their behavior and role within the dynasty or troop begins to shift. While still respected to a degree, elderly individuals face physical decline and reduced influence. Females become elders after 20 clutches, and suffer reduced fertility - with all future clutches producing a maximum of 2 eggs, regardless of season. When the mother reaches elder status, she becomes increasingly aggressive after repeated failed or smaller clutches. Nesting attempts from other females may be swiftly interrupted. Both males and females grow slower in movement as they age, and activity levels drop. They have shorter bursts of activity, and struggle to jump or climb as high as they could previously. They increasingly prefer warmer locations, and cuddle closer to other Deinonychus for warmth during the Rainy Season. Sparring matches between females become routinely forfeited from, with elder females not able to match the strength and stamina of a younger opponent. Elder males can become more irritable as their energy and stamina levels drop. They require soothing from their male companions, and more reassurance and grooming as they struggle to reach places on their bodies. A dynasty can be online and in game without the mother present. In her absence, a favored daughter takes the helm and guides the dynasty. A maximum of 10 Unrelated males can be part of a dynasty at a time. A mother may temporarily exile members for disobedience. This member can remain within the group if related (or as an unrelated male if there is space) but must keep their distance, until the mother is ready to re-accept them. Deinonychus may only hunt during the day, but can hunt outside of their hunting schedule if the target is albino, on deathscars, or hatchling/juvenile. Deinonychus are noisy dinosaurs. Broadcast calls :broadcast_call:  may be frequent. Deinonychus use broadcast calls :broadcast_call: to signal success, call for others, and announce a threat. Granddaughters are not permitted to nest. They may attempt to sneaky nest, but must disperse their offspring. If they nest at the same time as their mother (a daughter) they may attempt to mix 1 offspring in their daughter's nest in order to pass their offspring off as grandchildren. If successful, the offspring may stay in the dynasty in the grandchildren rank. This must be noted clearly in the bloodline log. Fletchlings are considered attended when they are fleeing with a fleeing Dynasty, even if they are not directly attended. Mothers may punish any individual in the dynasty as she deems fit, and chooses who gets to remain within the dynasty. Females may nip at other females and males for any reason, but may not go further than 2 bites unless directly sparring with another female and posturing has occurred. You can never challenge the mother for her position. Males must always submit to females in a dynasty and may never aggress others of their kind, unless encountering unrelated and unattended offspring. Males would rather shun individuals or flee from situations that would normally require aggression from them. Rat Out is not permitted to be used. DRM Dalmation is not always considered Albino-appearing.

Deinonychus hunting unattended and unrelated offspring of other Deinonychus or Kelenken offspring do not abide by the body down rule 5.1 Deinonychus have no species timer when challenging and chasing Latenivenatrix out of the POI. 6.2 When in a territory challenge with a rival dynasty, Deinonychus does not follow regular territory challenge rules and must follow proper posturing steps before the challenge begins. 6.7

solo.note: Gut solo spielbar: Das Profil sieht einzelne Deinonychus ausdrücklich vor. Sie bleiben leise und vorsichtig, folgen Herden und Apex-Räubern und leben vor allem von Aas. Allein jagst du bis Medium und darfst dich an jedem Räuberfang bedienen.

playstyle.summary: Du bist eine Tüpfelhyäne im Taschenformat mit dem Lärm einer Zwergmangusten-Bande. Solo bist du aber der stille Außenseiter: ein kleiner, cleverer Tagjäger, der großen Herden und Apex-Räubern mit Abstand folgt, auf Reste wartet und sich durch Beobachten, Geduld und Versuch und Irrtum durchschlägt. Du jagst und machst Kadaver nur tagsüber streitig, nachts darfst du alles andere tun. Vor Quetzalcoatlus und Hatzegopteryx fliehst du, Latenivenatrix meidest du allein. Wo die Dynastien laut, zickig und hierarchisch sind, bist du der wortkarge Überlebenskünstler.

parts.title: Alltag: Umherziehen, Beobachten, Schlafen
parts.text: Du bist Nomade im offenen und bewaldeten Gelände: Dry Fang Canyon, Steep Run, Black Fern Hills, Wind Tunnels und Hollow Hills sind offen, Cedrus Forest, Big Tree Overlook, Twisted Forest und die Redwoods bewaldet. Tagsüber hängst du dich an eine große Herde oder einen Apex-Jäger, zum Beispiel einen Rex oder einen Giga, und hältst genug Abstand, um sofort fliehen zu können. Wie eine Hyäne wartest du auf den Moment, in dem etwas für dich abfällt. Du beobachtest viel, lernst das Verhalten anderer Arten und übst dich an Kleintieren. In Ruhephasen erkundest du die Gegend und machst Lärm gegen alles, was deinem Rastplatz zu nahe kommt. Solo bist du aber deutlich leiser als eine Dynastie. Als Männchen kannst du dich später einer Troop anschließen oder dich geduckt einer Dynastie vorstellen. Als Weibchen kannst du nur mit einem Männchen deine eigene Dynastie gründen.

parts.title: Jagd & Aas
parts.text: Solo lebst du hauptsächlich von Aas: Allein oder zu zweit darfst du an jedem Räuberfang mitfressen, ohne den Kadaver erst streitig zu machen. Ab drei Tieren nur noch an Apex-Fängen. Kleintiere und verlassene Kadaver sind immer frei, und in der Not frisst du sogar Insekten. Jagen darfst du nur tagsüber, allein bis Medium, und Tenontosaurus ist deine Lieblingsbeute, wenn er in Reichweite ist. Unbewachte, fremde Jungtiere unter Adolescent darfst du jederzeit töten, ohne Timer und ohne Hunger- oder Tageszeit-Regeln. Unbewachte Kelenken-Junge darfst du ebenso töten, aber du fliehst, wenn ein Erwachsener zurückkommt. Apex-Sauropoden jagst du nie. Aasfresser an deinem eigenen Fang duldest du nicht. Metriacanthosaurus-Kadaver machen dich krank. Ein cleverer Trick aus dem Profil: Eine brütige Citipati-Henne adoptiert dich vielleicht, und die Herde, mit der sie zieht, wird dein Jagdrevier.

parts.title: Partnersuche & Balz
parts.text: Die Balz läuft wie im Profil und ist in einer Dynastie Sache der Mutter. Als Männchen gewinnst du Gunst durch Ducken, Putzen und Geschenke, am besten eine Jagdtrophäe. Das Weibchen fordert dich auf, indem sie die Arme ausbreitet und sich im Kreis dreht, und du richtest dich auf und machst es nach. Enkelinnen und Nichten dürfen nicht nisten. Genistet wird in Höhlen oder an Klippen zwischen dicken Farnen. Solo musst du dafür einer Dynastie beitreten oder, als Weibchen, mit einem Männchen eine eigene gründen.

analog.label: Spotted hyena + Dwarf mongoose
analog.headline: A spotted-hyena clan shrunk to mongoose size: noisy, female-ruled and deadly in numbers.
analog.playsLike: You are a small, extremely aggressive raptor in a 'dynasty' ruled by the Mother, and only her daughters and sisters may nest. Females bully and spar for status, while males are submissive, gift-giving and gentle; all-male 'troops' are cooperative. Numbers are everything: alone you hunt up to Medium tier, 4 hunt Large, and a full party of 8 hunts Apex. You also scavenge and cull unrelated, unattended young.

setting.label: Nomad of open and wooded ground
setting.note: Diurnal hunter and nomadic. Some individuals stay solitary and trail large herds or Apex carnivores to scavenge.

analogs.covers: Society and diet: female-ruled matrilineal clan, bullying females, submissive males, hunts and scavenges

relatives.name: Maip
relatives.headline: A bone-crunching, night-shrieking hyena pair with a raven's cruel intelligence.

analogs.covers: Scale and breeding: a tiny, noisy mob where only the dominant female's line breeds

why.text: Dominant, hyper-aggressive females ranked by favour with the Mother, and low-ranking, submissive males. Spotted-hyena clans work this way (official inspiration).
Granddaughters and nieces who nest are exiled, just as dwarf mongoose and meerkat groups let only the dominant female's line breed (official inspiration).
Solo animals and pairs may scavenge from any kill, groups of 3+ only from Apex kills. Hyenas both hunt and steal.
Small tier and 800 combat weight, yet with 8 in the party it can take Apex prey. Sprint 1,100 held for 200 s.
Attempts to cull unrelated, unattended offspring without timers or hunger requirements.

notLike: Spotted hyenas are big bone-crushers; Deinonychus is small and wins only through numbers.
Mongoose groups are cooperative; Deinonychus females are constantly scheming against each other.
analog.officialInspiration: hyenas, meerkats, red-necked phalaropes & common dwarf mongoose
